issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of natural disaster. Generic sensory cues can fit disaster trauma, but snakes and babies are highly specific cues with no clear link to a natural disaster and, taken together with body odour, suggest unrelated trigger themes rather than a single trauma network.

Within the overall profile, the memory/appraisal content is also mismatched. 'Intense shame on recall' usually implies a strong negative appraisal/self-evaluative theme, yet no Negative Appraisals items are endorsed and that node is formulation-wise disconnected. For a natural disaster survivor, shame can occur, but as the only explicit meaning-based memory item it sits awkwardly with otherwise cue-driven fragmented recall and no corresponding appraisal content.

'Babies' as an auditory trigger is hard to reconcile with a natural-disaster trauma in this profile unless there is specific undisclosed trauma content involving infants; the other triggers (loud noises, sweat/body odour) are more disaster-congruent, so this item stands out as clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking conflict/create drama' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The formulation links triggers mainly with memory and only minimally with maladaptive strategies, and the other selected items suggest intrusive sensory recall rather than an anger/interpersonal-dysregulation pattern. This coping item appears to target a symptom style not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: 'Sexual coping' is likewise poorly supported by the rest of the profile. With no threat or negative appraisal content selected and memory items focused on fragmentation/triggered recall, this strategy lacks a clear cognitive-affective anchor in the chosen profile and is difficult to connect specifically to natural-disaster PTSD here.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, sweat/body odour and alcohol smell are hard to link plausibly as primary trauma reminders unless there is additional disaster-specific context (e.g., shelter crowding, intoxicated bystanders). Loud noises fit, but these two olfactory triggers are clinically difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

Intense shame on recall is not impossible after a natural disaster, but as the only affective memory item here it is a poor fit with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes sensory triggering and fragmented involuntary recall rather than self-blame, humiliation, or morally charged memory content. This makes the memory node less coherent with the trauma type and the selected triggers/strategies.

Alcohol smell is a hard-to-explain trigger for a natural-disaster trauma in the absence of any matching trauma context or linked appraisal content; loud noise and smoke are coherent disaster-related cues, but alcohol odor stands out as clinically implausible here.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Intense shame on recall is not impossible after a natural disaster, but with no negative-appraisal content and no other memory material suggesting shame-linked actions or moral failure, this item is poorly supported and clinically discordant with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Alcohol Use: drink alcohol
issues.explanation: Using alcohol can occur nonspecifically, but paired with an alcohol-smell trigger it implies trauma meaning centered on alcohol-related cues that is not represented elsewhere in the disaster-based trigger or memory profile, reducing coherence.

vignette:
Carlos, a 40-year-old surgeon, had always prided himself on his ability to remain calm in the face of emergencies. Yet, ever since the devastating earthquake that struck his hometown in Latin America two years ago, he found himself grappling with an internal chaos that seemed to overshadow his once-steady demeanor. The quake had come without warning, collapsing buildings, uprooting lives, and claiming too many souls. Carlos vividly remembered the moment the ground had shaken violently beneath his feet, the sound of glass shattering, and the acrid smell of smoke enveloping him as he ran to help those trapped. Those sensory memories haunted him, and they were triggered often and unexpectedly. Even the faintest sound of a loud noise or the whiff of burnt wood would send him spiraling back to that day, his heart racing as the world around him blurred into the chaos of the disaster. After those memories surfaced, he noticed that even the most ordinary stimuli felt like alarms he couldn't ignore, compelling him to seek out distractions to escape the emotional flood. In those moments, the overwhelming sensations triggered a desperate urge to escape, leading him to drink or immerse himself in his work to dull the intensity of the memories.

In the months following the event, Carlos struggled to cope with the memories that surfaced without invitation. He found that the loud noises of everyday life - a siren wailing, a door slamming, or even the sound of thunder - could instantly transport him back to the earthquake's horror. After these memories surfaced, even the most ordinary stimuli felt like alarms he couldn't ignore, compelling him to seek out distractions like drinking or immersing himself in work to escape the emotional flood. The memories rushed in like a tide, overwhelming him with grief and anxiety. Because the memories came back so vividly, he found himself scanning his environment for familiar sounds that reminded him of the disaster, heightening his anxiety and leading to a desperate need to avoid those triggers. As the vividness of those memories intensified, he found that everyday sounds-like a siren wailing or a door slamming-triggered a sense of panic, propelling him towards his maladaptive strategies. Because the memories came back with such intensity, even the most ordinary things - the sound of a siren or the slamming of a door - felt like alarms he couldn't ignore, compelling him to seek out distractions to escape the emotional flood. He would often find himself momentarily frozen, unable to recall the full picture of what had happened, just fragments that filled him with shame and sorrow. It was as if the effort to avoid confronting those memories only kept them fresh and intact, making them louder and more vivid when they finally resurfaced. The more those intrusive memories surfaced, the more he felt compelled to distract himself; it was as if the mere thought of facing them pushed him to seek out anything that could provide a temporary reprieve. Because the memories rushed in with such vividness, even the most ordinary sounds - a siren wailing or a door slamming - felt like alarms he couldn't ignore, causing his heart to race and his mind to spiral back into the chaos of that day. Because these intrusive memories surfaced with such vividness, even ordinary stimuli became triggers, reminding him of the chaos and fear he had experienced during the earthquake. In these moments, he would feel a desperate need to escape the pain; the grief that washed over him was relentless and suffocating.

To manage the distress, Carlos turned to maladaptive strategies. He often distracted himself with work, pouring hours into surgeries and patient care, but even that was a temporary reprieve. He would sometimes indulge in drinking, believing that alcohol would help him forget the memories threatening to engulf him. However, each time he drank to escape, he noticed that the memories returned even stronger and more fragmented, as if his avoidance had only kept them fresh and intact, ready to erupt when he least expected it. The more he engaged in these maladaptive strategies, the more he realized that each act of avoidance only intensified the memories, leaving them unprocessed and lingering just beneath the surface. However, each time he drank to escape, he found that the memories returned even stronger and more fragmented, as if shoving them away only made them more insistent and palpable in his mind. The more he turned to drinking or immersing himself in work, the more the memories remained unprocessed, lingering just beneath the surface, waiting to erupt when he least expected it. On particularly difficult nights, he would find himself lost in sexual fantasies, using them as a way to release the tension that built up inside. Each coping mechanism offered fleeting relief, but they ultimately served to cloud his mind further, preventing him from processing the grief and trauma that lay beneath. Yet, the more he distracted himself with alcohol or fleeting fantasies, the more fragmented and unprocessed the memories became, lingering just beneath the surface, ready to erupt at any moment. He had been avoiding any mention of the earthquake for so long that when the memories finally surfaced, they felt louder and more vivid than ever, as if all that suppression had only kept them fresh and unprocessed in his mind. As he engaged in these distractions, Carlos felt guilt and confusion, knowing that they kept him from confronting the memories he so desperately needed to face.

Despite the temporary relief these maladaptive strategies provided, they did nothing to quell the intrusive memories. In fact, each time Carlos drank or allowed himself to escape into fantasies, he felt an increasing sense of disconnection from the reality of the earthquake. The more he avoided confronting the trauma, the more fragmented his recollection became. He would often tell himself he was fine, yet that very denial only deepened the chasm within him, making the memories sharper and more painful when they inevitably returned. He would recall the faces of those who had perished, the cries for help, and the ash that lingered in the air, and with each recollection, the cycle of avoidance tightened its grip.

Now, two years later, Carlos found himself at a crossroads. His marriage was beginning to suffer; his wife, feeling the distance he had created, urged him to seek help. He could no longer deny the toll the trauma had taken on his life and his relationships. As he sat in the waiting room of the clinic, the sounds of the bustling city outside felt like a cacophony of reminders, amplifying his anxiety. What frightened him most was the thought of facing the earthquake again - the memories flooding back, the grief overwhelming him. Yet, beneath that fear was a flicker of hope: perhaps by confronting the trauma, he could begin to reclaim the life he had lost and the love he had almost allowed to slip away.

  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."

  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."

  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Carlos, a 40-year-old surgeon, had always prided himself on his ability to remain calm in the face of emergencies. Yet, ever since the devastating earthquake that struck his hometown in Latin America two years ago, he found himself grappling with an internal chaos that seemed to overshadow his once-steady demeanor. The quake had come without warning, collapsing buildings, uprooting lives, and claiming too many souls. Carlos vividly remembered the moment the ground had shaken violently beneath his feet, the sound of glass shattering, and the acrid smell of smoke enveloping him as he ran to help those trapped. Those sensory memories haunted him, and they were triggered often and unexpectedly. Even the faintest sound of a loud noise or the whiff of burnt wood would send him spiraling back to that day, his heart racing as the world around him blurred into the chaos of the disaster. After those memories surfaced, he noticed that even the most ordinary stimuli felt like alarms he couldn't ignore, compelling him to seek out distractions to escape the emotional flood. In those moments, the overwhelming sensations triggered a desperate urge to escape, leading him to drink or immerse himself in his work to dull the intensity of the memories.

In the months following the event, Carlos struggled to cope with the memories that surfaced without invitation. He found that the loud noises of everyday life — a siren wailing, a door slamming, or even the sound of thunder — could instantly transport him back to the earthquake’s horror. The memories rushed in like a tide, overwhelming him with grief and anxiety. As the vividness of those memories intensified, he found that everyday sounds—like a siren wailing or a door slamming—triggered a sense of panic, propelling him towards his maladaptive strategies. Because the memories came back with such intensity, even the most ordinary things — the sound of a siren or the slamming of a door — felt like alarms he couldn't ignore, compelling him to seek out distractions to escape the emotional flood. He would often find himself momentarily frozen, unable to recall the full picture of what had happened, just fragments that filled him with shame and sorrow. It was as if the effort to avoid confronting those memories only kept them fresh and intact, making them louder and more vivid when they finally resurfaced. The more those intrusive memories surfaced, the more he felt compelled to distract himself; it was as if the mere thought of facing them pushed him to seek out anything that could provide a temporary reprieve. Because the memories rushed in with such vividness, even the most ordinary sounds — a siren wailing or a door slamming — felt like alarms he couldn't ignore, causing his heart to race and his mind to spiral back into the chaos of that day. Because these intrusive memories surfaced with such vividness, even ordinary stimuli became triggers, reminding him of the chaos and fear he had experienced during the earthquake. In these moments, he would feel a desperate need to escape the pain; the grief that washed over him was relentless and suffocating.

To manage the distress, Carlos turned to maladaptive strategies. He often distracted himself with work, pouring hours into surgeries and patient care, but even that was a temporary reprieve. He would sometimes indulge in drinking, believing that alcohol would help him forget the memories threatening to engulf him. However, each time he drank to escape, he noticed that the memories returned even stronger and more fragmented, as if his avoidance had only kept them fresh and intact, ready to erupt when he least expected it. However, each time he drank to escape, he found that the memories returned even stronger and more fragmented, as if shoving them away only made them more insistent and palpable in his mind. The more he turned to drinking or immersing himself in work, the more the memories remained unprocessed, lingering just beneath the surface, waiting to erupt when he least expected it. On particularly difficult nights, he would find himself lost in sexual fantasies, using them as a way to release the tension that built up inside. Each coping mechanism offered fleeting relief, but they ultimately served to cloud his mind further, preventing him from processing the grief and trauma that lay beneath. Yet, the more he distracted himself with alcohol or fleeting fantasies, the more fragmented and unprocessed the memories became, lingering just beneath the surface, ready to erupt at any moment. He had been avoiding any mention of the earthquake for so long that when the memories finally surfaced, they felt louder and more vivid than ever, as if all that suppression had only kept them fresh and unprocessed in his mind. As he engaged in these distractions, Carlos felt guilt and confusion, knowing that they kept him from confronting the memories he so desperately needed to face.

Despite the temporary relief these maladaptive strategies provided, they did nothing to quell the intrusive memories. In fact, each time Carlos drank or allowed himself to escape into fantasies, he felt an increasing sense of disconnection from the reality of the earthquake. The more he avoided confronting the trauma, the more fragmented his recollection became. He would often tell himself he was fine, yet that very denial only deepened the chasm within him, making the memories sharper and more painful when they inevitably returned. He would recall the faces of those who had perished, the cries for help, and the ash that lingered in the air, and with each recollection, the cycle of avoidance tightened its grip.

Now, two years later, Carlos found himself at a crossroads. His marriage was beginning to suffer; his wife, feeling the distance he had created, urged him to seek help. He could no longer deny the toll the trauma had taken on his life and his relationships. As he sat in the waiting room of the clinic, the sounds of the bustling city outside felt like a cacophony of reminders, amplifying his anxiety. What frightened him most was the thought of facing the earthquake again — the memories flooding back, the grief overwhelming him. Yet, beneath that fear was a flicker of hope: perhaps by confronting the trauma, he could begin to reclaim the life he had lost and the love he had almost allowed to slip away.
